prompt: Blog post: 'The tests are the documentation' is a lie we tell ourselves. Make it opinionated but not ranty.
a:
The claim sounds hard-nosed: prose documentation drifts out of date, but tests are code, so they're always current. Read the tests and you'll know what the code does.

It's an appealing idea, and it isn't entirely wrong. Tests are precise in a way prose rarely is, and a good test suite shows concrete examples of how an API is meant to be called. But as a replacement for documentation, it falls apart quickly.

Start with readability. Tests are written to exercise code, not to explain it. They're full of setup, fixtures, mocks and helper functions, and the interesting line is often buried under thirty lines of scaffolding. A newcomer trying to understand what a module does has to reverse-engineer intent from a pile of assertions, which is slower and more error-prone than reading a paragraph someone wrote for them.

Then there's organization. Documentation is structured for a reader: overview first, details later. Tests are structured for a test runner. They're grouped by file, by class, sometimes by whichever developer added them, and there's no natural reading order. You can't skim a test suite the way you can skim a README.

The bigger problem is that tests go stale just as easily as docs do. A test written three years ago for a feature that has since been redesigned may still be sitting there, quietly describing behavior nobody cares about anymore, and newer developers have no way of knowing it's obsolete. The promise that tests stay in sync with the code turns out to be about as reliable as the promise that someone will update the wiki.

Finally, tests only cover what someone thought to test. Large parts of a typical codebase have thin coverage, and in those areas the tests, as documentation, say nothing at all.

None of this means tests are useless for understanding code. They're valuable, and when you want to know exactly how a function handles an edge case, a well-named test is often the fastest answer. But they work best alongside real documentation, not instead of it.

The fix isn't complicated. Keep a short README for each significant module that explains what it does and how to use it. Write docstrings for public functions. Give tests descriptive names so they read like specifications. And make updating documentation part of the definition of done for any change, so it gets reviewed along with the code.

Tests tell you that code works. Documentation tells you how to use it. A healthy project needs both, and pretending one can do the other's job just leaves future readers to fill in the gaps on their own.
b:
The claim sounds hard-nosed: prose documentation drifts out of date, but tests run on every commit, so they can't lie. Read the tests and you'll know what the code does.

The second half of that is true, and it's exactly why the first half fails. Tests tell you what the code does in the cases someone thought to write down. They don't tell you which of those behaviors are promised.

Here's the problem in miniature. You find a test asserting that `get_orders()` returns orders sorted by date. Is sorting part of the contract, something callers rely on and you must preserve? Or did the author sort the result to make the assertion deterministic, and the order is an accident of the current query? The test passes either way. It cannot tell you which. Multiply that by a few thousand assertions and you have a precise, executable record of current behavior with no way to separate the load-bearing parts from the incidental ones. That distinction is the single most important thing documentation is for.

Tests also can't say why. A test can pin down that retries stop after three attempts. It can't tell you that the limit exists because the upstream payment provider rate-limits at four, and that raising it will get your account suspended. The next engineer, reading only the test, sees an arbitrary number and a test to update.

And tests can't describe what isn't there. Non-goals, rejected designs, the thing that looks like a bug but is deliberate: these live in people's heads or nowhere. A suite of examples is silent on everything outside the examples, and silence reads as permission.

None of this means tests are bad documentation. They're the best evidence you have, because evidence that runs is worth more than evidence that merely claims. But evidence isn't explanation. The fix is cheap and boring. Write a short paragraph at the top of each module saying what it promises, what it deliberately doesn't do, and why the odd constraints exist. Name tests after the contract they enforce ("returns orders newest first, callers depend on this") rather than the mechanism. When a test exists only to pin down incidental behavior, say so in a comment, so the next person knows they're allowed to break it.

Tests answer "what does it do right now?" with total reliability. Documentation answers "what am I allowed to change?" Teams that treat the first as the second end up afraid to touch anything, because every passing assertion looks like a promise. Write down which ones actually are.

prompt: I'm a self-taught developer and I still feel like a fraud because I never learned data structures properly. I've shipped real products for 5 years. I'd like an essay about what CS fundamentals actually buy you in day-to-day work, honestly, without either reassuring me falsely or gatekeeping.
a:
Here is the honest version: computer science fundamentals matter, but probably less than you fear and differently than the gatekeepers suggest. Five years of shipping real products is not nothing, and it's worth taking that evidence seriously before deciding you're a fraud.

Start with what fundamentals are often credited with. Classic data structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash maps, graphs) and the algorithms that go with them form the core of most CS curricula. They teach a way of thinking about problems: breaking them down, reasoning about trade-offs, and choosing the right tool. Graduates come away with a shared vocabulary, which makes it easier to read technical papers, follow conference talks, and communicate with colleagues who went through the same training.

They also matter, frankly, for hiring. Many companies still run whiteboard interviews built around these topics, and if you ever want to move to a large tech company, you will likely need to practice them. That's a real cost of skipping them, even if it says more about interviewing than about the job.

In day-to-day work, though, the picture is different. Most of what a working developer does is integrating libraries, modeling business logic, handling edge cases, talking to APIs, and keeping a codebase readable for the next person. Your language's standard library already provides well-optimized collections, and your database handles the heavy lifting of storage and retrieval. With modern hardware as fast as it is, the difference between an elegant algorithm and a naive one rarely shows up at the scale most products run at; it matters mainly for companies operating at enormous volume. That's why so many self-taught developers build successful careers without ever formally studying algorithms.

Where fundamentals help most is in the occasional hard problem: something that needs to be fast, or something that resembles a well-known puzzle. In those moments, having the background lets you recognize the pattern rather than reinventing it. But those moments are relatively infrequent, and when they come up, the information is a search away.

So what should you do? If the feeling bothers you, spend some time filling in the gaps. A structured course or a few months working through practice problems can give you confidence and the vocabulary to hold your own in technical discussions. Treat it as professional development rather than penance.

And remember that imposter syndrome is extremely common in this field, including among people with degrees from excellent universities. Feeling like a fraud is not evidence that you are one. The products you've shipped, the bugs you've fixed, and the users who rely on your work are the better measure. Fundamentals are a useful tool to add to your kit, not a test you failed by learning in a different order.
b:
Here is the honest version: fundamentals buy you less than the people who gatekeep with them claim, and something more specific than the people who dismiss them admit. Five years of shipping tells you the first part already. The second part is worth naming exactly, because once it's named it stops being a vague cloud of fraudulence and becomes a gap with edges.

What you almost never need is to implement a red-black tree, a heap, or a hash table. Your language and your database did that, better than you would, and nobody will ask you to redo it at work. If your sense of fraud is pinned to that, unpin it. Most working engineers with CS degrees couldn't write a balanced tree from memory either.

What fundamentals actually give you is a cost model: the ability to look at code and predict how it will behave when the input is a hundred times bigger. That shows up constantly in ordinary work, disguised as other things. It's the loop that calls `list.contains` inside another loop and is fine with 200 records and dead with 200,000. It's the page that makes one database query per row. It's knowing that a database index is a sorted structure, so it helps with equality and ranges and prefixes but not with `LIKE '%foo'`. It's choosing a set instead of a list without thinking about it. None of these feel like "data structures" when you hit them. They feel like "the app got slow in production and I spent a week finding out why."

The second thing fundamentals buy is recognition. Some problems have a known shape: this is a graph traversal, this is a scheduling problem, this is a cache with an eviction policy, this is actually a solved problem with a forty-year-old algorithm. People with the vocabulary recognize the shape and look up the answer. People without it often build something that works, more slowly, and sometimes something subtly wrong.

So here is a test that's fairer than any credential. When you write code, can you say roughly how its time and memory grow with the input, and do you know which operations on your main collections are cheap and which are expensive? Do you know what your database does with your queries? If yes, you have the part of the fundamentals that matters day to day, and where you got it is irrelevant. If no, that's the precise gap, and it is small: a few weeks with a good algorithms text, focused on complexity, hashing, trees, and graphs, will close most of it. You don't need the proofs. You need the intuitions.

The fraud feeling, I suspect, comes less from the gap itself than from not knowing how big it is. Unknown unknowns feel bottomless. Measured, this one isn't. You have five years of evidence that you can build things people use. What's left is learning to see the costs that were always there, and that is a finite project, not a verdict.

prompt: My grandma is 84 and still does tai chi in the park every morning. She says that's why she's never fallen. Is there actually something to that or is she just lucky and stubborn?
a:

It also makes sense mechanically: the slow weight shifts, single-leg stances and turns train exactly the balance, leg strength and quick corrections that tend to fade with age. Some studies also suggest benefits for confidence, since people who are afraid of falling tend to move less, which makes them weaker and more likely to fall.

The fair caveat is that the arrow runs both ways. Anyone who gets to the park every morning at 84 is already unusually healthy and mobile, so part of her record is likely the underlying health that lets her do tai chi in the first place, not only the tai chi itself. Researchers try to control for this in trials, but in any one person's life it's impossible to fully separate the two.

Still, roughly one in four Americans over 65 falls each year, so "never fallen at 84" is a genuine achievement, and her habit is very likely helping. And the stubbornness counts as well, honestly. The hardest part of any exercise program, at any age, is showing up every single day, and she clearly has that part figured out.

prompt: Argue that the best software in the world is boring internal tooling nobody outside the company ever sees.
a:

prompt: why do people say you shouldn't eat right before swimming? is the cramp thing real or just something parents made up
a:

Digestion does send extra blood to your gut. However, your body has more than enough blood to supply both your stomach and your muscles. There are no documented cases of someone drowning because of a full stomach. The American Red Cross asked its scientific advisory council to review the claim. The council found no evidence supporting the cramp story. Doctors who study drowning report similar conclusions. They point to alcohol, fatigue, and cold water as the real dangers.

That said, there is a smaller real effect. If you swim hard right after a large meal, you may get a side stitch. You may also feel sluggish or nauseous, and in some cases you might vomit. These effects are uncomfortable and might make you want to stop. However, they will not make your legs stop working. A gentle swim after eating is fine. Intense racing is less advisable, for the same reason you wouldn't sprint after a big holiday dinner.

The rule has survived because it is harmless and somewhat useful. It gives children a mandatory break, and it gives adults some time to rest. The version worth keeping is about alcohol rather than food. Alcohol is a real factor in a large share of adult drownings.

prompt: Could you explain how a mortgage amortization schedule works, specifically why the early payments go almost entirely toward interest? I'd appreciate a short worked example.
a:
An amortization schedule is a table that shows, for each payment over the life of a loan, how much goes to interest and how much goes to principal. The key point is that each month's interest is charged only on the balance you still owe, while the total payment stays the same. Early on, the balance is at its largest, so interest takes most of the payment and only the remainder reduces the loan. As the balance gradually falls, the interest portion shrinks and the principal portion grows.

Here is a worked example. Suppose you take out a $300,000 loan at a fixed 6 percent annual rate for 30 years. The monthly rate is 6 percent divided by 12, or 0.5 percent, and the fixed payment works out to $1,798.65.

- Month 1: interest is 0.5% of $300,000, or $1,500.00. Only $298.65 goes to principal, leaving a balance of $299,701.35.
- Month 2: interest is 0.5% of $299,701.35, or $1,498.51. Principal is $300.14.

As you can see, the balance is falling by only about $300 a month, so the interest charge barely changes from one month to the next. The principal portion doesn't overtake interest until month 223, more than eighteen years into the loan. Over the full term, you would pay roughly $347,500 in interest, more than the original amount borrowed.

It's worth noting that actual figures will vary with your rate, term, and lender, and that property taxes and insurance collected through escrow are not part of this calculation. This pattern is also one reason extra payments early in the loan can be so effective: every dollar of principal you retire in the first year stops accruing interest for the remaining 29 years.

prompt: I'd love a short essay arguing that the best way to see a city is to run errands in it. Like actually needing to buy batteries or get a haircut.

prompt: I read that you should never use git rebase because it destroys history and that's why our team only does merge commits. Can you explain why rebase is so dangerous so I can explain it to the new hire?
a:
Rebase isn't dangerous in the way you've heard, and I'd hate for the new hire to learn a myth on day one. Here's the real version.

Rebase doesn't destroy history so much as rewrite it. It takes your commits and replays them on top of another branch, creating new commits with new IDs. The old ones aren't deleted right away. Git keeps them in the reflog, by default for about 90 days, so a botched rebase can almost always be undone with `git reflog` and a reset.

The real danger is narrower. If you rebase commits other people have already pulled, their copies and yours now disagree about what happened. Push that with `--force` and you can overwrite a teammate's work on the shared branch. That's the whole rule: don't rebase commits someone else may have built on.

On your own unpushed branch, though, rebase is safe and often useful. Squash your "fix typo" commits. Pull in the latest main before opening a pull request. Plenty of teams that only merge into main still let people rebase locally all day.

So your team's merge-only policy can be perfectly reasonable. Merge commits keep a record of exactly when branches came together, and they're harder to get wrong. Just give the new hire the accurate reason: it's a choice about shared history, not a safety measure against a dangerous tool.

What I'd tell them is short. Rebase your own branch whenever you like. Never rebase main. If you ever do need to force-push, use `--force-with-lease`, which refuses to overwrite commits you haven't seen.

You should not rebase commits that someone else may have built on.

On your own unpushed branch, however, rebase is safe and often useful. You can use it to squash small "fix typo" commits. Additionally, you can use it to pull in the latest main before opening a pull request. Moreover, many teams that only merge into main still allow people to rebase locally.

Your team's merge-only policy can still be reasonable. Merge commits keep a record of exactly when branches came together. Furthermore, merge commits are harder to get wrong. However, the new hire should hear the accurate reason. The policy is a choice about shared history. It is not a safety measure against a dangerous tool.

In summary, the guidance for the new hire is simple. They can rebase their own branch whenever they like. They should never rebase main. Additionally, if they need to force-push, they should use `--force-with-lease`. This option refuses to overwrite commits they have not seen.

prompt: why do clocks on old microwaves and ovens drift but my phone never does
a:
Two different reasons depending on the appliance, and in neither case is the clock bad at counting. It's that nothing ever corrects it.

Many ovens and microwaves count the cycles of your AC power: 60 per second in North America, 50 in most other places. Grid operators keep that frequency accurate enough over time that these clocks can be pretty good, but a power blip stalls or resets them, and when the grid runs off-frequency, they drift with it. In 2018 a dispute in the Balkans held the European grid slightly low for weeks, and oven clocks across much of the continent ran about six minutes slow.

Others run on a cheap quartz crystal. Those are typically accurate to around 20 parts per million, which comes to roughly a minute a month, uncorrected forever.

Your phone's crystal isn't meaningfully better. The difference is that the phone keeps checking: it takes the time from your carrier's network and from internet time servers, which are tied to atomic clocks, and quietly resets itself. It drifts like anything else; it just gets fixed long before the error adds up to a second.

Which kind your microwave is depends on the model. If it only loses time after the power flickers, it's probably counting the grid.

So the microwave is a watch nobody ever sets. The phone is a watch that checks with an atomic clock all day.
b:
There are a number of factors that could be at play here, and it really depends on the specific appliance.

Some older microwaves and ovens may use the frequency of the AC power supply to keep time, while others might rely on an internal crystal oscillator of some kind. In the case of grid-based clocks, the accuracy can potentially be affected by fluctuations in the power grid, though how much this matters likely varies by region and by utility. There have been reports of grid-related clock drift in some places, though it's hard to generalize from those cases.

Crystal-based clocks, on the other hand, can drift to varying degrees depending on the quality of the components, temperature, age, and other variables. Cheaper parts may be less precise, but it's difficult to say exactly how much drift you should expect without knowing the specific hardware involved.

Phones, by contrast, generally tend to sync their time with external sources, such as the cellular network or internet time servers, which may help keep them accurate. That said, phones aren't necessarily immune to drift either; it's possible that they drift as well but are simply corrected often enough that you don't notice.

Ultimately, the answer probably comes down to some combination of the timekeeping method used, the quality of the hardware, and whether the device has any way of correcting itself. If you're curious about your particular microwave, the manual might offer some clues, or you could try observing whether it seems to lose time after power interruptions.

prompt: Why does every city seem to think it's the 'Paris of' somewhere? Paris of the Midwest, Paris of the East, Paris of South America. Is there any city that gets called the something-else of Paris?
a:
It's a fun question, and the answer mostly comes down to what Paris stands for in the popular imagination. For a couple of centuries Paris has been shorthand for beauty, romance, art, fashion and good food. When a city calls itself the Paris of somewhere, it's borrowing all of those associations at once, which is a lot more efficient than listing them.

Tourism has a lot to do with it. Travel writers and city boosters love a quick hook, and "the Paris of South America" tells a reader in five words that Buenos Aires has elegant architecture, cafe culture and a lively arts scene. Shanghai, Hanoi, Beirut and Bucharest have all worn some version of "Paris of the East" for similar reasons, usually because of French influence on their buildings or their culture.

As for the reverse, it basically doesn't happen, and the reason is fairly simple: Paris is unique. No other city has quite the same combination of history, culture and beauty, so there's nothing to compare it to. You could imagine someone calling Paris "the New York of Europe" for its energy, but it has never caught on, because Paris already has such a strong identity of its own that it doesn't need to borrow one.

Other cities get used the same way, though less often. Venice is the big one, with plenty of "Venices of the North," and Edinburgh has long been called the Athens of the North. But Paris remains the most popular reference point, probably because its image is so broad that almost any attractive, cultured city can claim a piece of it.
b:
Because the phrase is a loan, and loans only flow one way.

"The Paris of the East" doesn't describe a city so much as stake a claim for it. Most of these nicknames date from roughly 1860 to 1930, when Paris, freshly rebuilt by Haussmann, was the world's model of what a modern capital looked like: wide boulevards, uniform stone facades, cafes, an opera house, department stores. Cities that got rich in that period often built to match, sometimes with French-trained architects. Buenos Aires really does have Parisian avenues and mansard roofs. Bucharest put up its own Arc de Triomphe. Detroit's radial avenues earned it "the Paris of the West." The nickname records a moment when a city was rising and wanted to say so in the most prestigious terms available.

That's why you almost never hear the reverse. Calling Paris "the Buenos Aires of Europe" would be lending prestige to the place that already had the most of it, which flatters Buenos Aires and tells you nothing about Paris. The construction "the X of Y" always points from a periphery toward a center. Venice works the same way, which is why there are a dozen Venices of the North (Amsterdam, Stockholm, St Petersburg, Bruges) and no Amsterdams of the South.

So the list of "Paris of" cities is really a map of where wealth and ambition were a century ago, drawn in someone else's vocabulary. Notice that the cities rising today rarely reach for it. Nobody calls Shenzhen the Paris of anything. The reference points have moved on: now a place wants to be "the Silicon Valley of" somewhere, or "the next Dubai."

prompt: Is there any point in making a teenager learn cursive in 2026? My dad is weirdly upset that my kids can't read his letters.
a:
Writing cursive, probably not much. Reading it, yes, and that's the part your dad is actually upset about.

The case for teaching teenagers to write in cursive is thin. The research people cite about handwriting helping memory compares writing by hand with typing; it doesn't show that joined-up letters beat printed ones. A teenager who prints legibly has most of whatever benefit handwriting offers. And nobody is going to need cursive for a job, a form, or a signature that a scribble won't cover.

Reading cursive is a different skill and a much cheaper one. A kid who can read print can learn to read most cursive in an afternoon or two, because it's mostly the same letters with connectors and a handful of odd capitals, the G, the Q, the loopy F. It also opens up more than you'd think: old family letters, recipe cards, a grandparent's notes in the margins of a book, and if they ever get curious, most of the historical record before about 1980.

Which brings it back to your dad. I'd guess his upset isn't really about penmanship standards. He's been writing to his grandkids in the hand he learned, the way people wrote to the ones they loved, and it turns out the letters can't be read. That stings in a way that's hard to argue with.

So a nice fix might be to have the kids learn to read his handwriting specifically, maybe with him. Have him read one letter aloud while they follow along. Within a couple of letters they'll have the hang of it, and he'll have gotten something better than being right.
b:
## Should Teenagers Learn Cursive?

**Short answer:** Writing it, probably not. Reading it, yes, and that's the part your dad is actually upset about.

### The case for writing cursive
- Research on handwriting and memory compares writing by hand with **typing**, not cursive with print.
- A teen who prints legibly gets most of the benefits handwriting offers.
- Cursive isn't needed for jobs, forms, or signatures.

### The case for reading cursive
- **It's quick to learn:** a kid who reads print can pick up most cursive in an afternoon or two.
- It's mostly the same letters with connectors, plus a few odd capitals (G, Q, F).
- **It opens doors:** old family letters, recipe cards, notes in the margins of books, and much of the historical record before about 1980.

### About your dad
- His upset probably isn't about penmanship standards.
- He's been writing to his grandkids in the hand he learned, and the letters can't be read.
- That's an understandable thing to feel hurt by.

### A suggested fix
1. Have the kids learn to read **his** handwriting specifically.
2. Do it together: he reads one letter aloud while they follow along.
3. After a couple of letters, they'll have the hang of it.

**Bottom line:** Skip cursive writing drills, but spend an afternoon on cursive reading. Your dad gets something better than being right.

prompt: how do people live with a decision they can't take back
a:
Mostly by ending the trial. In the months after a decision like that, the mind keeps reconvening court. It replays the moment, introduces new evidence, argues the case again in the hope of a different verdict. That is exhausting, and it never ends in acquittal, because the one thing this court cannot do is change what happened.

What seems to help people is remembering who actually made the call: someone working with what they knew then, at that hour, frightened or tired or out of time. You know things now that they didn't. Judging them by it is a little like blaming yourself for not having read tomorrow's paper. That doesn't make the decision right. Sometimes it wasn't. But "I chose badly" is a sentence a person can live inside. "I should have known" usually isn't, because it is so rarely true.

The other thing people do, eventually, is stop trying to set the decision down and start carrying it. Regret held long enough tends to turn into a kind of care. You hold the next hard choice more gently. You are kinder to the next person standing where you stood. That isn't redemption, exactly. It's what the weight becomes once you stop fighting it.

prompt: Write an essay ranking nothing, just defending the honor of the sport everyone makes fun of: curling. Earnestly.
a:
Curling is often mocked, and to some extent that's understandable, though many people would argue the sport deserves more respect than it gets. Whether it is truly as difficult as other sports is hard to say, since difficulty depends a lot on how you define it, but there are certainly aspects of curling that may be more challenging than they first appear.

Consider the stone. Curling stones are fairly heavy, generally somewhere in the range of 40 pounds or so, and they are often made of a special kind of granite, some of which reportedly comes from Scotland. The ice is also not entirely smooth, from what players describe, and that may affect how the stone moves in ways that are not always easy to predict. Delivering a stone accurately over a long distance is arguably a real skill, though of course how impressive that is may depend on one's perspective.

Sweeping is another element that is sometimes misunderstood. It appears that sweeping can influence the stone's path and distance, possibly by changing the ice surface in some way, although the exact effects can vary depending on conditions, technique, and other factors. Some might say this makes curling more of a team sport than it looks, while others may see it as a minor detail.

Strategy also seems to play a role. There is something called the hammer, which is the last stone of an end, and it is generally considered an advantage, though how much it matters likely depends on the situation and the skill of the teams involved. Some commentators have compared curling to chess, which may or may not be a fair comparison, but it does suggest that there is more thinking involved than many people assume.

Interestingly, the physics of why stones curl is apparently still debated, which could indicate that the sport is more complex than it seems. However, it's also possible that this reflects the difficulty of studying ice more than anything special about curling itself.

Perhaps the most commonly praised aspect of curling is its culture of sportsmanship. Players are often said to call their own fouls, and conceding a game is generally seen as respectful rather than shameful, at least in many contexts. Of course, every sport has its own traditions, and it would be hard to say definitively that curling is more sportsmanlike than others.

In the end, whether curling deserves its reputation is probably a matter of personal taste. It may not be for everyone, and there are reasonable arguments on both sides. But for those willing to give it a closer look, there may well be more to appreciate than the jokes suggest.
b:
Curling is mocked for the reason chess would be if it were televised from directly overhead: the hard part is invisible. What you see is a person sliding gently, a stone drifting, two people sweeping like they're late for a dinner party. What you're watching is one of the most exacting sports there is.

Start with the stone. It is about 42 pounds of granite, the best of it quarried on Ailsa Craig, a lump of an island off the Scottish coast, because that granite resists both chipping and water. Only a narrow ring on its underside, about the width of a pencil, touches the ice. And the ice is not smooth. Before play it is sprayed with droplets that freeze into tiny bumps called pebble, and the stone rides across their tops. The thrower has to send it the length of the sheet, well over a hundred feet, and stop it within inches of where the skip asked, with exactly the right spin.

The sweepers are not decoration. Brushing hard in front of the stone warms and polishes the pebble, cutting friction, so the stone travels farther and curls less. Two sweepers judging speed by eye, a skip reading the line from the far end, everyone shouting: no other sport lets a team steer a shot after it has been taken.

Then there is the strategy, which is real. The team with the last stone of an end, the hammer, holds an advantage so large that a good team will sometimes deliberately score nothing rather than take a single point, just to keep it. Every throw reshapes the geometry for every stone after it. Players set guards they mean to curl around three shots later, and a stone left an inch too deep can decide a game an hour on.

One honest admission: physicists still argue about exactly why a stone curls in the direction it spins, and why it curls as much as it does. A sport that has resisted a complete explanation through a century of scientific attention has earned some respect for that alone.

But the best case for curling is its manners. At most levels there are no referees. Players call their own fouls; if you brush a moving stone, you say so. When a team knows it can't win, it concedes with a handshake, and that is considered the gracious thing rather than quitting. At the club level, the winners traditionally buy the losers a drink.

Here is a sport that asks for millimeter precision, tactical patience and plain honesty, and then asks you to be nice about it. People laugh because it looks easy. Try it once. Your first stone will either die a third of the way down the sheet or sail through the house and out the back, and you will stop laughing.

prompt: Why are train stations so much nicer than bus stations? Not just in the US, seemingly everywhere. I want an essay that actually tries to answer it.
a:
Start with the tracks. A railway is about the most committed thing a city can build: once a line runs into a particular plot of land, it will run there for a century or more, because moving it would mean rebuilding everything behind it. A station at the end of that line is the safest long-term investment imaginable, and the people who built the great ones knew it. A bus, by contrast, can stop anywhere there is a curb. Its terminal is provisional by nature, and you can feel the provisional in the architecture: the low roof, the strip lighting, the sense that the whole operation could move across town next year.

Then look at when the stations were built. Most of the beautiful ones date from roughly 1850 to 1930, when railways were the most advanced technology on earth and the companies that ran them were among the richest. Stations were their advertising. Rival lines into London, Paris and New York built cathedrals partly to outshine each other, and they could afford to, because stone and labor were cheap and the railways owned the land. Intercity buses matured later, in the age of the car, as the cheaper alternative to something else. Nobody builds a monument to the cheaper alternative.

That word, cheaper, explains most of the rest. In much of the world the bus is how you travel when you can't afford the train or the plane, and spending follows the customer. Bus operators run on thin margins and are often several small companies sharing a terminal that the city owns and treats as a cost to be kept down. A railway, especially a state one, usually owns its station outright and can pay for its upkeep with shops, offices and the land around it. Grand Central earns its keep as a market, a food hall and a landmark, not only as a place to catch a train.

Location compounds it. Trains need their own right of way, so the lines were cut into city centers early and the stations became the city's front door. Buses use the same roads as everyone else, so their terminals could be pushed out to the edge of town, onto cheap land near the highway. A front door gets dressed up. A loading dock doesn't.

The exceptions prove the rule from both sides. When New York decided in 1963 that Penn Station was merely a place to change trains, it tore down a masterpiece and put up a basement, and the result was as grim as any bus depot. And where buses are how a whole country travels, as in Turkey or much of Latin America, the big intercity terminals are busy, well kept and often perfectly pleasant, with real restaurants and real waiting rooms.

So the difference isn't really about trains and buses. It's about commitment and status. A train station is a fixed bet made in a prosperous era for a mode of travel that once carried everyone. A bus station is a flexible arrangement for a mode many people use only when they have to. Buildings tend to look like the promises behind them.
b:
# Why Train Stations Are Nicer Than Bus Stations

Train stations are often grand, beautiful buildings, while bus stations tend to be functional at best and grim at worst. This pattern holds in many countries, and several factors explain it.

## 1. Permanence

- **Tracks are fixed.** Once a rail line runs into a city, it stays for a century or more, because moving it would mean rebuilding everything behind it.
- **Stations are long-term investments.** A station at the end of a permanent line is a safe place to spend money.
- **Buses are flexible.** A bus can stop anywhere there is a curb, so bus terminals feel provisional: low roofs, strip lighting, and a sense the operation could move next year.

## 2. Historical Timing

- **The golden age of rail.** Most beautiful stations were built between roughly 1850 and 1930, when railways were cutting-edge technology and rail companies were extremely wealthy.
- **Stations as advertising.** Rival lines into London, Paris and New York built grand stations partly to outshine each other.
- **Cheap materials and labor.** Stone and labor were inexpensive, and railways owned the land.
- **Buses came later.** Intercity buses matured in the age of the car, as a cheaper alternative, and nobody builds monuments to the cheaper alternative.

## 3. Economics and Ownership

- **Who rides matters.** In much of the world, the bus is how people travel when they cannot afford the train or plane, and spending follows the customer.
- **Thin margins.** Bus operators are often small companies sharing a city-owned terminal that is treated as a cost to minimize.
- **Railways own their stations.** They can fund upkeep through shops, offices and surrounding land. Grand Central, for example, earns money as a market, food hall and landmark.

## 4. Location

- **City center vs. city edge.** Rail lines were cut into city centers early, so stations became the city's front door.
- **Buses use public roads.** Bus terminals could be pushed to the edge of town, onto cheap land near highways.

## 5. Exceptions

- **Penn Station.** In 1963 New York demolished its magnificent Penn Station and replaced it with a basement-like facility as grim as any bus depot.
- **Bus-centric countries.** In Turkey and much of Latin America, where buses are the main way people travel, large intercity terminals are busy, well kept and often pleasant.

## Conclusion

Ultimately, the difference is not really about trains versus buses but about **commitment and status**. A train station is a fixed bet made in a prosperous era for a mode that once carried everyone, while a bus station is a flexible arrangement for a mode many people use only when they have to. In short, buildings tend to reflect the promises behind them.

prompt: My kid is 8 and has started reading graphic novels exclusively, like Dog Man on loop, and the other parents at school talk about it like it's junk food. I read comics as a kid and I turned out fine (I think?). But I also notice I can't concentrate on long books anymore and wonder if that started somewhere. Can you write a thoughtful essay on whether it matters what kids read as long as they read? Something I could maybe share with the other parents, not preachy.
a:
Every generation has a format that makes adults nervous. Our parents' friends worried about comics. Their parents worried about pulp magazines. Somebody in the eighteenth century worried that novels would rot young minds. The worry always has the same shape: the child is enjoying this too much for it to be good for them.

Dog Man on loop looks like junk food from across the room, but up close it's doing real work. A comic asks a reader to hold words and pictures together, to infer what happened between panels, and to track who is speaking and in what tone, without a narrator to explain. That is reading. The looping isn't a bad sign either. Children reread the way they rewatch and replay: to get fluent, to catch the jokes they missed, to enjoy being good at something. An eight-year-old who knows a book cold is practicing the part of reading that later becomes automatic.

What a steady diet of graphic novels doesn't build by itself is stamina: staying with a long page of unillustrated text, picturing things no one drew, carrying a plot across a week. That's a separate skill, and the honest answer to "does it matter what they read" is that it matters less what they read than whether something is stretching them. The easy way to stretch an eight-year-old isn't to take Dog Man away. It's to read aloud to them from books a little above their level, and to leave a few such books lying around. Most kids drift toward longer books once they've already tasted the pleasure of one.

As for those of us who read comics and now can't finish a novel, I'd look at the phone before the childhood. The attention most adults have lost was lost recently, a scroll at a time, and comics didn't do that. The cure is the same as for the kid: time, quiet, and a book worth staying with.

So let them have Dog Man. Read them something else at bedtime. And maybe put your own phone in another room for an hour and see what happens.

prompt: blog post: what my Quaker meeting taught me about sitting in silence with 40 strangers. I've been going for 2 years, not a believer exactly. Want it to be honest about the boring parts too
a:
The first thing nobody tells you about Quaker meeting is how long an hour is.

## How It Works

I started going two years ago, mostly out of curiosity and partly because I wanted somewhere to be on Sunday mornings that wasn't my phone. The meeting I attend is "unprogrammed":

- No minister, no sermon, no music
- About forty of us on wooden benches, facing each other, in a plain room
- Anyone who feels moved to speak stands, says something, and sits down (most weeks two or three people do; some weeks nobody does)
- At the end of the hour, one person shakes the hand of the person next to them, and then everybody does

I'm not a believer, exactly. Friends talk about "that of God in everyone," and I don't know what I think about that. Nobody has ever asked me to.

## The Boring Parts (Let's Be Honest)

There are a lot of them. For the first twenty minutes my mind is a radio stuck between stations: the grocery list, an email I should have sent, the man two benches over who clears his throat every ninety seconds. My left foot falls asleep. Some of what people stand up to say is wonderful, and some of it is a long account of their tomatoes, or a political opinion in very thin disguise. There are weeks when the whole hour is the grocery list, and I leave feeling like I've sat in a waiting room.

## What I've Learned

What keeps me going back is harder to name, but here's my best attempt:

1. **Silence with other people is not the same as silence alone.** Alone, I drift. In that room, forty people are attempting the same difficult, slightly ridiculous thing, and their attention holds mine up a little, the way it's easier to stay on pace when someone is running beside you.

2. **Much of what I say could go unsaid.** In meeting, you only stand if the words won't stay down. I've started noticing, at work, how often I talk just to fill a gap, and how rarely the gap needed filling.

3. **Boredom is often a door, not a wall.** The restlessness usually comes right before something settles. Not every week, and not on command. But sometimes, around minute thirty-five, the room changes. Quakers call it a "gathered" meeting, when the silence seems to deepen all at once and everyone feels it. I've felt it maybe four times in two years.

4. **Intimacy without information.** I know only a handful of names in that room. I know how a lot of the others sit, which ones close their eyes, who cries sometimes, whose knees crack when they stand.

## Final Thoughts

I don't know if what happens there is God. I know it is the only hour of my week when I'm not trying to be anywhere else, and that most weeks it's at least a little bit boring. I've come to think those two facts are related.

prompt: Why is it so hard to get someone off a sex offender registry or to expunge an old conviction, even when everyone agrees the person isn't dangerous? Is there a design reason or is it just politics?
a:
Great question! This is a complex issue that touches on law, public policy, and politics. The short answer is that it's a mix of both design and politics. Let's break it down.

**Why Removal From a Sex Offender Registry Is Difficult**

- **Offense-based tiers:** Under the federal Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA), the length of registration is determined by the offense of conviction rather than an individual risk assessment. Tier I lasts 15 years, while Tier III lasts for life.
- **Civil, not criminal:** In Smith v. Doe (2003), the Supreme Court ruled that registration is a civil regulatory measure rather than punishment. This limits the constitutional protections available to registrants.
- **Political incentives:** Officials face significant risk if someone they remove reoffends, but little consequence for keeping low-risk individuals on the registry.

**Why Expungement Is Difficult**

- **Petition process:** In many states, people must file a petition, pay fees, and sometimes attend a hearing. Research in Michigan found that only about 6.5% of eligible individuals obtained expungement within five years.
- **Private databases:** Even after a record is expunged, it may persist in commercial background-check databases.
- **Reform efforts:** "Clean slate" laws, first passed in Pennsylvania in 2018, automatically seal eligible records to address these barriers.

**Is It Design or Politics?**

Ultimately, it's both. These systems were intentionally designed to prioritize public safety and minimize discretion, and that design reflects the political climate in which the laws were passed.

**In summary**, the difficulty stems from a combination of offense-based legal structures, court decisions, political risk aversion, and administrative hurdles.

I hope this helps! If you'd like, I can walk you through the specific process in your state or summarize recent reform efforts.
b:
Mostly design, though the design was itself a political choice made in a particular mood.

Registries were built in the 1990s and 2000s after a run of horrifying, heavily covered crimes against children, and the laws carry those children's names: Jacob Wetterling, Megan Kanka, Adam Walsh. Legislators weren't designing a system for weighing individual risk. They were designing one that would never again let a known offender slip past, and the surest way to guarantee that is to make placement automatic and removal rare. Under the federal framework, how long you stay on is set by the offense you were convicted of, not by any assessment of who you are now. Tier I is fifteen years; Tier III is life. A judge who thinks you're harmless often has no lever to pull.

The courts helped lock this in. In 2003 the Supreme Court held that registration is a civil regulatory measure, not punishment, which means most of the protections that come with punishment don't apply.

Then there's the asymmetry behind every one of these decisions. If a judge or legislator lets someone off and that person reoffends, there's a name and a headline. If they keep a thousand harmless people on, the cost is spread thin and nobody is blamed for it. Any official facing those incentives says no.

Expungement has a different problem: friction. Most states make you petition, which means forms, fees, often a lawyer, and a hearing. When economists studied Michigan, they found only about 6.5 percent of eligible people got their records cleared within five years. That's why "clean slate" laws, starting with Pennsylvania in 2018, seal eligible records automatically. And even a cleared record can live on in private background-check databases that copied it years ago.

So it's not a conspiracy, but it's not an accident either. The system does what it was built to do.

prompt: I'm a hardware engineer and I understand caches at the silicon level. What I don't get is why software people talk about 'cache-friendly data structures' as if they control that. Like what in a C++ program actually changes how the L1 gets used?
a:
Software doesn't control the cache. It controls the address stream, and the cache's behavior is a function of that stream. "Cache-friendly" means writing code whose stream has good locality and a pattern the prefetcher can follow. In C++ the levers are layout and order.

Contiguity. A std::vector<int> puts elements at consecutive addresses, so one 64-byte line brings in sixteen of them and the stride prefetcher stays ahead. A std::list or std::map allocates each node separately, wherever the allocator finds room, so traversal becomes a chain of dependent loads to unpredictable addresses. Same big-O, often several times slower.

Struct layout. If a loop reads only each particle's position but each Particle is 128 bytes, most of every fetched line is wasted. Splitting fields into separate arrays (structure of arrays), or moving rarely used fields out of the hot struct, makes every fetched byte count.

Traversal order. C arrays are row-major, so a loop whose inner index walks down a column strides a full row per access and touches a new line every time.

Size. Four-byte indices instead of eight-byte pointers, or float instead of double where precision allows, fit twice as many elements in L1.

Sharing. Two threads writing different variables that sit in the same line will bounce it between cores. Padding them apart with alignas(64) stops the false sharing.

None of this touches the hardware. It changes which addresses get requested, in what order, and how densely the useful bytes are packed.
b:
Software doesn't actually control the cache in any direct sense. There's no instruction in a typical C++ program that says "put this in L1." What software does control is the stream of addresses the CPU requests, and since the cache's behavior is a deterministic function of that stream, the programmer's choices end up shaping hit rates quite a lot. So when software people say "cache-friendly," what they really mean is code whose address stream has good spatial and temporal locality and a pattern the prefetcher can recognize. In C++, the main levers are data layout and access order.

Contiguity. A std::vector<int> stores its elements at consecutive addresses, so a single 64-byte line brings in sixteen of them, and the stride prefetcher can stay ahead of the loop. By contrast, a std::list or std::map allocates each node separately, wherever the allocator happens to find room, which means traversal turns into a chain of dependent loads to essentially unpredictable addresses. Both may have the same big-O complexity on paper, but in practice the node-based version is often several times slower, and sometimes much worse.

Struct layout. Suppose a loop reads only each particle's position, but each Particle struct is 128 bytes because it also holds velocity, color, mass, an ID and so on. Then most of every fetched line is wasted on fields the loop never touches. Splitting the fields into separate arrays (structure of arrays), or moving rarely used fields out of the hot struct, means every byte you fetch is a byte you use.

Traversal order. C and C++ arrays are row-major, so if your inner loop walks down a column of a 2D array instead of along a row, each access strides by a full row and lands on a new cache line every time. Swapping the loop order can make a dramatic difference.

Size. Using four-byte indices instead of eight-byte pointers, or float instead of double where the precision allows, lets you fit twice as many elements in L1.

Sharing. When two threads write different variables that happen to sit in the same cache line, the coherence protocol bounces that line between cores. Padding the variables apart, for example with alignas(64), eliminates this false sharing.

Of course, the exact benefits will vary by microarchitecture, compiler and workload, so it's always worth profiling. But the common thread is that none of this touches the hardware at all. It simply changes which addresses get requested, in what order, and how densely the useful bytes are packed into each line.

prompt: My brother-in-law swears premium gas makes his Honda Civic run better. The manual says regular. He says he can 'feel the difference'. Is there anything to this or is it pure placebo?
a:
It's almost certainly placebo, and the reason comes down to what octane actually measures.

Octane isn't a measure of energy or quality. It's a measure of how well fuel resists igniting from compression alone, before the spark plug fires; when that happens too early, you get knock. Premium and regular contain essentially the same energy per gallon, so a higher number on the pump doesn't mean more power in the cylinder. Engines that require premium have high compression or turbochargers that squeeze the mixture hard enough to need the extra resistance. The Civic isn't one of them. Honda designed and tuned it to make its rated power on 87.

There's also a simple way to know his engine isn't secretly benefiting. If the Civic were knocking on regular, the knock sensor would detect it and the check-engine light would come on. Since his car runs on regular without any warning lights, the engine is already getting everything it needs, and the extra octane has nothing to do.

So what is he feeling? Probably expectation. He paid more and he's paying attention, and that's enough for most people to notice a smoother idle or a quicker response that isn't really there. It's the same reason wine tastes better when you know it was expensive.

The practical point is cost. Premium usually runs 70 cents to a dollar more per gallon, which adds up to a few hundred dollars a year for no measurable benefit. If he wants to spend money on his Civic's fuel system, buying gas from a Top Tier detergent brand will do more good than buying a higher grade.
b:
Mostly placebo, with one small real effect he almost certainly isn't feeling.

Octane isn't energy. It's a measure of how well fuel resists igniting under compression before the spark plug fires; that early ignition is knock. Premium and regular hold essentially the same energy per gallon. Higher octane only helps an engine built to use it, with high compression or heavy turbo boost, where the computer would otherwise have to pull back the ignition timing to stop knock. Honda tuned the Civic to make its rated power on 87. On regular it isn't knocking, so there's nothing for premium to fix.

The small real effect: on the turbocharged Civics, the engine computer adjusts timing on the fly, and on a hot day at full throttle it can sometimes take a little more advance with premium. Dyno tests occasionally show a few percent more power near the top of the rev range. But he'd have to be flooring it to get there, and nobody can feel a few percent from the driver's seat.

What he can feel is expectation. He paid more, he's listening for a difference, and the brain is generous about supplying one. That's not an insult; everyone's perception works that way.

The fair way to settle it is a blind test. Have someone else fill the tank for a month or two, switching grades without telling him, and have him write down after each tank which one he thinks it was. If he beats a coin flip by much, I'd be surprised. Meanwhile he's paying something like 70 cents to a dollar more per gallon for the feeling.

prompt: I spent two full days chasing a bug that turned out to be a trailing whitespace in an environment variable. TWO DAYS. I feel like an idiot. does this happen to experienced people or am I just bad at this
a:
It happens to experienced people all the time. Invisible-character bugs are a classic precisely because they defeat the normal way of debugging: you print the value, it looks right, you compare it by eye to what it should be, it looks right. What experience changes isn't whether you hit this bug. It's how long it takes. That's what you just bought with those two days. It's an expensive lesson, but it's a permanent one.

Two cheap habits that would have caught it: strip whitespace when you read config, and validate config at startup so a bad value fails loudly at boot instead of mysteriously downstream.

You're not bad at this. You found it.
b:
It's hard to say for sure, since it depends a lot on the person and the situation, but bugs like this can happen to people at many different experience levels. Invisible-character issues can be tricky because they may not show up when you print a value, and the value might appear correct at a glance, so it's understandable that it could take a while.

Some people might argue that more experienced developers would catch something like this sooner, and in some cases that may be true, since they may have encountered similar problems before. Others would say that everyone runs into these kinds of issues from time to time, regardless of experience. There are a lot of factors involved: the tools you're using, how the environment is set up, how much time pressure you're under, and so on.

There are a few practices that some developers find helpful in situations like this, such as printing values with delimiters (for example `echo "[$VAR]"` or `print(repr(x))`), stripping whitespace when reading configuration, or validating config at startup. Whether these would have helped in your case would depend on the specifics.

As for whether you're bad at this, it's probably not productive to draw conclusions from a single incident. Debugging skill can vary a lot, and many factors contribute to how long a bug takes to find. It might be worth reflecting on what you learned and seeing how it goes next time.

prompt: How does your body know when to stop growing taller? What actually tells the bones to quit?
a:
It's generally thought that the bones stop growing when the growth plates close, and hormones, likely including estrogen, seem to play an important role in that process, though the full picture is complicated.

Each long bone, like the femur, has areas of cartilage near the ends called growth plates. Cells there divide and are gradually replaced by bone, which is believed to be how most of the lengthening happens. Height depends largely on this process, along with many other factors.

Several things may contribute to the process slowing down. The plates may have something like a built-in limit, with cells gradually losing their ability to divide, which could help explain why growth tends to slow in childhood. Puberty also seems to be involved: rising hormone levels appear to cause a growth spurt and, at some point, may contribute to the plates being replaced by bone. When that happens, the plate is considered "closed." The timing varies quite a bit between individuals, but it often happens somewhere in the mid-to-late teens, perhaps a little earlier for girls.

Interestingly, estrogen may be relevant in boys too, since testosterone can be converted into it. Some research on rare conditions suggests that people who can't respond to estrogen may keep growing longer than usual, although these cases are uncommon and may not apply to everyone.

Of course, genetics, nutrition, overall health, and other hormones like growth hormone likely all play a part, and researchers are still learning about the details. So the answer depends on a number of interacting factors, and there probably isn't one single thing that tells the bones to quit.
b:
The bones stop because the growth plates close, and the main signal that closes them is estrogen, in boys as well as girls.

Each long bone, like the femur, has a disc of cartilage near each end called a growth plate. Cells in the plate divide, stack into columns, swell, and are replaced by bone, which pushes the end of the bone outward. Height comes almost entirely from this process in the legs and spine.

Two things shut it down. First, the plates have a built-in clock: their cells gradually lose the ability to divide, which is why growth slows steadily through childhood even before puberty. Second, at puberty, rising estrogen speeds growth up for a couple of years (the growth spurt) and then drives the plate to finish its program and be replaced entirely by bone. Once that happens the plate is "closed" and the bone can't lengthen any more. In girls that's usually around 14 to 16; in boys, around 16 to 19.

Boys get their estrogen by converting testosterone. The clearest evidence for this comes from rare men who can't make estrogen or can't respond to it: they keep growing slowly into their twenties and thirties, with open plates, and end up very tall. Giving the ones who lack estrogen the hormone closes their plates.

What's still not fully understood is what sets the pace of that built-in clock in the first place. Genes clearly matter, since height is highly heritable, but the cellular mechanism of the countdown is an open research question.

prompt: Could you explain how a pumped hydro storage plant works and how it compares with lithium-ion batteries in terms of duration and round-trip efficiency? A brief comparison of the two would be helpful.
a:
A pumped hydro storage plant uses two reservoirs at different elevations. When there is surplus electricity on the grid, often at night or during sunny and windy periods, the plant pumps water from the lower reservoir to the upper one. When demand rises, it lets the water flow back down through turbines, generating electricity much as a conventional hydroelectric dam does. In effect, it stores electricity as the gravitational potential energy of water.

Lithium-ion batteries store energy chemically, shuttling lithium ions between electrodes as they charge and discharge. They are compact and modular and can be installed quickly, which is why grid-scale battery deployment has grown so rapidly over the past decade.

On duration, pumped hydro has the edge. A plant can typically generate for 6 to 12 hours, sometimes longer, while lithium-ion batteries deliver their energy over about 1 to 4 hours, because the chemistry is best suited to short, intense bursts of power rather than slow, sustained discharge.

On round-trip efficiency, batteries come out ahead, returning roughly 85-90% of the stored electricity compared with around 70-80% for pumped hydro. Batteries also respond almost instantly, though their cells degrade over 10 to 20 years, whereas pumped hydro plants can operate for half a century or more but require specific geography and long construction periods.

Overall, pumped hydro offers longer duration and a longer life, while batteries offer higher efficiency and more flexibility in where and how quickly they are built. With battery costs continuing to fall and their efficiency advantage likely to persist, batteries seem set to take a growing share of new storage, while pumped hydro remains valuable where suitable sites already exist.
b:
A pumped hydro plant is two reservoirs at different heights joined by a tunnel, with a machine at the bottom that works as a pump in one direction and a turbine in the other. When electricity is cheap or in surplus, the plant pumps water uphill; when power is needed, the water falls back through the turbine and generates it. The energy is stored as height, so how much you have is set by how much water the upper reservoir holds and how far it can fall.

That detail is the key to the comparison. In pumped hydro, power (how fast you can deliver, set by the turbines) and energy (how long you can keep going, set by the reservoir) are bought separately, and once the turbines exist, extra hours mostly cost a bigger pond. So plants are typically built for 6 to 12 hours at full output, and a few for days. In a lithium-ion system, every additional hour means proportionally more cells, so cost rises almost linearly with duration. That, rather than anything in the chemistry, is why nearly all grid batteries are sized for 1 to 4 hours.

On round-trip efficiency, batteries win: roughly 85-90% of the electricity put in comes back out, against about 70-80% for pumped hydro, which loses energy in the pumps, turbines, generator and pipes. Batteries also respond in milliseconds and can be built in months almost anywhere.

Pumped hydro answers with duration and longevity: plants run for 50 years or more, while battery cells degrade over 10 to 20. Its handicaps are geography and lead time; you need the right terrain, water and permits, and often close to a decade.

In short, batteries are the better tool for shifting energy across a few hours and steadying grid frequency; pumped hydro remains the cheaper way to store large amounts of energy for a day or more. They are complements more than rivals.

prompt: What I wish I knew about forgiveness before I tried to do it. Write this as a personal essay. Context: I spent about two years 'forgiving' my brother for something, announced it to him, and then realized I hadn't. Turns out forgiveness isn't a decision. Or is it? You tell me.
a:
For about two years I was forgiving my brother. I want to be precise about the tense, because that's where the trouble was. I thought of it as something I was doing, like a degree, and one Sunday on the phone I announced I had finished. "I forgive you," I said, with the satisfaction of a man returning a library book. He said thanks. Then he mentioned the thing he'd done, in passing, the way you'd mention the weather, and I felt the old heat climb my neck as if nothing had happened in two years. Which, it turned out, was about right.

So I did what you do: I read about it, and the consensus was humbling. Forgiveness, it turns out, isn't a decision. It's a process, and processes don't take orders.

I had treated it like a New Year's resolution, something you declare and then simply are. But you can decide to go to the gym; you can't decide to be fit. Forgiveness is the fit part. It happens to you, gradually, as a result of time and reflection and, if you're lucky, a few honest conversations. No amount of announcing speeds it up.

The other thing everyone says, and I've come around to it, is that forgiveness is really for yourself. Resentment is drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die. My brother, for his part, seemed fine. I was the one rehearsing arguments in the shower. Whatever forgiveness is, its main beneficiary was always going to be me.

So where I went wrong was the announcement. I declared victory over a feeling I still had, and the feeling, reasonably, called my bluff. Real forgiveness, I've decided, is the kind that holds when it's tested. If the anger comes back the moment he brings it up, then whatever I'd been doing for two years wasn't forgiveness yet. It was a ceasefire I had mistaken for peace. The honest move is to wait until the mention of it lands softly, and only then say the words.

That's a humbling standard, and I'm not there. Some days I think I'm close; then a holiday comes around and I'm not. I've stopped trying to rush it. I journal a little. I've talked about it with a friend who has her own version of my brother. I try to notice the resentment without scolding myself for it, which is harder than it sounds.

I also want to say that forgiveness isn't the same as excusing what happened. It was wrong, and I can hold that while still hoping to let go of the anger.

So, is forgiveness a decision? You asked me to tell you, so I will: no. It's something that arrives when it's ready, and the most you can do is make room for it. I made the mistake of thinking I could schedule it. Next time, if there's a next time, I'll keep my mouth shut until I actually feel it, and let the forgiving speak for itself.
b:
For about two years I was forgiving my brother. I want to be precise about the tense, because that's where the trouble was. I thought of it as something I was doing, like a degree, and one Sunday on the phone I announced I had finished. "I forgive you," I said, with the satisfaction of a man returning a library book. He said thanks. Then he mentioned the thing he'd done, in passing, the way you'd mention the weather, and I felt the old heat climb my neck as if nothing had happened in two years. Which, it turned out, was about right.

So I did what you do: I read about it. The popular line is that forgiveness isn't a decision, it's a feeling that arrives when it's ready, and you can't force it. This is comforting, and I think it's half wrong.

Here is what I believe now. We use one word for two things. One is a decision: I give up my claim. I won't collect the debt, won't bring it out as ammunition, won't arrange family Christmas so that he has to feel it. That part is entirely in my power, and I can do it on a Sunday. The other part is the feeling, the resentment itself, and that is not in my power at all. It follows the decision slowly, the way your body follows you into cold water, and it may never fully arrive.

My mistake wasn't deciding. It was announcing the second part when I'd only done the first. I told him the account was closed, emotionally speaking, when what I had actually done was stop charging interest. Those are different things, and he deserved to know which one he was getting. So did I.

Seeing it this way changed what the relapse meant. When the anger came back on the phone, I took it as proof that I'd failed and the two years were a fraud. But resentment flaring up isn't a verdict on the decision. It's the occasion for it. The part of forgiveness you control isn't one act; it's a habit of declining, each time the old grievance shows up with its bill, to pay it. You forgive the second time, and the eleventh. The feeling gets quieter, not because you willed it, but because you stopped feeding it.

It also untangled something I'd confused for years. Forgiving him is not the same as trusting him, and neither is the same as pretending it was fine. I can give up the debt and still not lend him money.

So, is forgiveness a decision? Yes, but not the one I thought. It isn't deciding to feel differently; you can no more do that than decide to be hungry. It's deciding how to act while you feel what you feel, and then deciding it again. If I announced anything now, it would be smaller and truer: I'm not holding it against you. I'm still working on not holding it.

prompt: why do swimmers shave their whole bodies, does a little hair really make a difference

Modern tech suits cover a lot of the body now, so the shave matters mostly for the arms, back and shoulders. For a recreational swimmer it makes no practical difference at all.

prompt: I used to love physics in school and then got lost in calculus and gave up. I'm 34 now. Is it possible to actually understand something like quantum mechanics without the math, or is everything popular science writers tell you basically a misleading metaphor?
a:
Yes, more than you'd probably think, and honestly the popular metaphors are a big part of why it feels so out of reach. It's very common to love physics in school and then hit a wall with calculus, and 34 is not remotely too late.

The core of quantum mechanics isn't actually calculus. At its heart, it's this: a quantum system is described by amplitudes, which are numbers attached to each possible outcome, and the probability of any given outcome is the square of its amplitude. Unlike ordinary probabilities, though, amplitudes can be negative (complex, really), which means two different routes to the same outcome can cancel each other out. That cancellation, which physicists call interference, is where nearly all of the strangeness lives. The double-slit pattern, entanglement, why measuring something changes what happens next: all of it follows, in one way or another, from adding amplitudes instead of adding probabilities.

The good news is that the math you'd need for the real thing is mostly linear algebra rather than calculus, and for simple systems, like the polarization of a single photon, it's roughly high-school level. It's worth looking for books that build quantum mechanics up from two-state systems rather than starting with waves. Of course, everyone learns differently, so it may take some trial and error to find the right one. But at 34, with some patience and curiosity, you can genuinely get inside it, and it might be even more rewarding now than it would have been in school.

prompt: I teach urban economics. I'm looking for a clear, non-technical explanation of agglomeration economies that I could give first-years before we get to the models — something with a concrete example that isn't Silicon Valley, which they've all heard.
a:
Start with a puzzle: why would competitors choose to sit next to each other? Rents are higher, they bid up each other's workers, and they can see each other's prices. Yet firms in the same line of business cluster all the time. Agglomeration economies are the name for the reason: being near many similar firms makes each one more productive, in ways no single firm could arrange for itself.

A good example is Dalton, Georgia, a small city in the Appalachian foothills that makes most of America's carpet. It began in the early 1900s with women tufting chenille bedspreads by hand; when the technique was mechanized after the war, the mills grew up where the know-how already was. Three forces kept them there:

- **Sharing.** A cluster of mills supports suppliers that one mill alone couldn't: yarn spinners, dye houses, backing makers, a repair shop that stocks the exact part for a tufting machine. Each mill gets cheaper, faster inputs.
- **Matching.** The people who know how to run and fix tufting machines live there. A mill that loses one can hire another by Monday, and a worker who loses a job can find a new one without moving house.
- **Learning.** Ideas leak. A new backing material or dyeing trick at one mill shows up down the road within a season, carried by suppliers, salespeople and people changing jobs.

The key word is *external*. None of these benefits is something a firm can buy or own; they come from the presence of the others. That's why a newcomer to the industry would rationally choose Dalton over a cheaper site, and why the cluster keeps reinforcing itself.

It's worth pointing out to students that Dalton is not a big city. The advantage comes from concentrating one industry, not from size in general, which sets up the later distinction between localization and urbanization economies.

prompt: In cricket, how does reverse swing work? I understand conventional swing (shiny side, rough side) but reverse swing seems to break that logic and every explanation I've found just says 'it's complicated'.
a:
It's a great question, and you're right that most explanations give up too early. The shiny-versus-rough story is a useful shorthand, but it isn't the underlying mechanism. What actually matters is where the air lets go of the ball.

As the ball flies, a thin boundary layer of air clings to its surface. If that layer is smooth (laminar), it peels away from the ball relatively early. If it's turbulent, it hugs the surface for longer before separating. This is the same reason golf balls have dimples: the dimples make the boundary layer turbulent so it stays attached longer and the ball carries farther.

In conventional swing, the angled seam trips the air on its side into turbulence, so that side holds on longer. Meanwhile the shiny side stays laminar and lets go early. Because the air leaves the two sides at different points, the wake behind the ball is asymmetric, and the ball is pushed toward the seam side. That's why keeping one side shiny matters: it keeps that side laminar.

Reverse swing happens when the air turns turbulent before it ever reaches the seam. Two things can cause that. One is real pace, something like 85 to 90 mph with a fairly new ball. The other is one side being so scuffed that the roughness itself trips the flow, which brings the required speed down considerably. That's why it tends to turn up with an old ball, often after 40 overs or so, on a dry, abrasive square, and why subcontinental conditions are associated with it.

Now both sides are turbulent, and the seam's role flips. Instead of tripping fresh laminar flow, it thickens a layer that's already turbulent, tiring it, so it separates earlier than on the other side. The seam side now lets go first, and the ball swings away from the seam, toward the shiny side.

So, to sum up: same grip, same seam angle, opposite swing. That's exactly what makes it so dangerous. A batter reading the wrist sees an outswinger and gets one that comes in. Hopefully that makes it feel a bit less like magic.
